challenges.name: ci-permissions-quiz
challenges.title: Who can reach this token?
challenges.description: Three pieces of evidence from the CI review: a preview workflow triggered by pull_request_target, a dependency resolved from the wrong registry, and the trust policy of the deploy role.

questions.question:
.github/workflows/preview.yml:

on: pull_request_target
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  preview:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npx vercel deploy --prebuilt --token "$VERCEL_TOKEN"
        env:
          VERCEL_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }}

Statement: "Because the workflow limits GITHUB_TOKEN to contents: read, a pull request from a fork cannot get VERCEL_TOKEN out of this workflow."
questions.explanation: False. The permissions block scopes only GITHUB_TOKEN; it has no effect on repository secrets such as VERCEL_TOKEN. pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository, so secrets are available even when the pull request comes from a fork, and this job then checks out the fork's commit and runs it: npm ci runs its install scripts and npm run build runs its build script. That code can rewrite node_modules/.bin/vercel or any file the last step uses, so the step that receives VERCEL_TOKEN executes code the fork controls. The fix is to build untrusted code with the pull_request trigger, which gives forks no secrets, and to deploy previews only for branches of the repository or from a separate privileged workflow that never executes the pull request's code. The misconception is that permissions: is a general sandbox; it limits one token.

True. A scope registry line sends every package of that scope to that registry and nowhere else; npm does not fall back to the default registry or compare versions across registries. Laptops were safe only because each developer's ~/.npmrc had the line; the CI runner has no such file, so it asked the public registry, where someone had published 2.99.0 - a version chosen to satisfy ^2.4.0. Put the line in the repository's .npmrc so every machine uses it, regenerate the lockfile and check that every @codedev entry's resolved URL points at npm.codedev.test, and claim the codedev organisation on npmjs.com so nobody else can publish under that scope. The misconception is that a higher version on the public registry wins over a correctly configured scope; it only wins when the scope is not configured.

questions.question:
Trust policy of the AWS role codedev-deploy:

"Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com" },
"Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
"Condition": {
  "StringEquals": { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com" },
  "StringLike":   { "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:codedev/platform:*" }
}

.github/workflows/deploy.yml - the only workflow that requests id-token: write:
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

Statement: "Because only the deploy workflow on main requests id-token: write, only runs on main can assume the codedev-deploy role."
questions.explanation: False. Which workflow requests id-token: write today is decided by files that anyone with push access can change: a developer can push a branch with a new workflow that requests the permission, and its token's subject (repo:codedev/platform:ref:refs/heads/that-branch, or repo:codedev/platform:pull_request for a pull_request run from a branch of the repository) matches repo:codedev/platform:*. The trust policy is the real boundary, and it accepts any ref, pull request or environment of the repository. Narrow it to repo:codedev/platform:ref:refs/heads/main, or better repo:codedev/platform:environment:production with required reviewers on that environment, and protect main so a workflow change needs review. OIDC removes long-lived keys; it does not remove the need to say exactly who may use the role. The misconception is that the workflow file, not the cloud-side condition, decides who gets credentials.
